medium.titulo: Come creare un calendario dell’avvento digitale
medium.resumo: Vuoi creare e condividere un calendario dell’avvento personalizzato coi tuoi amici? Questa è la guida che fa al caso tuo!
medium.conteudo_html:
Ehi! Se nel corso della lettura dovessi avvertire un senso di smarrimento (in alcuni rari casi anche crampi alle dita dei piedi) puoi scrollare in fondo e visionare un fantastico video nella speranza che sia più chiaro dell’articolo!

È novembre, fa un certo freschino, quando usciamo di casa usiamo le calze di spugna anzichè i collant da cinque denari e, inevitabilmente, il Natale si avvicina.
In questo periodo una delle tradizioni che più amo è il calendario dell’avvento, be’, diciamo che amo il cioccolato, ma visto che il calendario dell’avvento contiene cioccolato… 🤷‍♂️
Tuttavia viviamo in un’epoca in cui sentiamo l’obbligo di digitalizzare qualunque cosa quindi un bel giorno mi sono prefissato l’obiettivo di creare un calendario dell’avvento digitale, da condividere con amici e familiari, dove dietro a ogni casellina si può nascondere un’immagine simpatica, un meme, una foto di Jessica Nigri o qualsiasi contenuto digitale.
Bye bye cioccolato, benvenuti pixel 👋

In questo articolo vi mostro come realizzare in pochissimi passaggi il VOSTRO calendario dell’avvento digitale 😎

1. L’idea alla base

Il concetto è semplice: un calendario dell’avvento digitale con 24 pacchetti numerati, uno per ogni giorno di dicembre fino alla vigilia.
I pacchetti si sbloccano solo il giorno corrispondente e, cliccandoci sopra, rivelano il contenuto nascosto.

Nel mio esempio qui sopra il 1° dicembre sarà possibile aprire il primo pacchetto e vedere l’immagine associata (si capisce che il suddetto pacchetto è attivo perchè si muove a destra e sinistra!)

Il 2 dicembre si sbloccherà anche il secondo pacchetto e così via fino al 24!

Una volta aperto un pacchetto si potrà visionare il suo contenuto 👇

2. La struttura del calendario

Dopo questa breve premessa passiamo alle cose serie.
A livello tecnico, il calendario dell’avvento è sviluppato in Vue.js, non c’è un motivo ben preciso legato a questa scelta, volevo solo provarlo.
Visita questo indirizzo https://codepen.io/LucaBn/pen/LYqbZzP (se vorrai condividere il tuo calendario personalizzato dovrai crearti un account su CodePen, ma tranquillo, è gratis).

Nelle prime tre righe del codice trovi tre variabili:

  • year
  • author
  • imgUrlList

Modificane il valore a tuo piacimento ricordandoti che la lista di URL deve contenere ventiquattro stringhe valide per funzionare!
Nel prossimo paragrafo ti spiegherò nel dettaglio come fare 😉

3. Personalizzazione delle immagini

Cambiare le immagini è facilissimo:

  1. Recupera 24 URL di immagini.
  2. Per esempio puoi usare Imgur per caricare le tue foto (mi sa che anche qui dovrai crearti un account gratuito!).
  3. Copia le URL e incollale nella lista imgUrlList.
  4. Salva, attendi che la pagina si refreshi… e voilà, i pacchetti conterranno le nuove immagini!

Ti fornisco qualche idea per le immagini da usare (non mi ringraziare, lo faccio con piacere):

  • Meme divertenti del gruppo WhatsApp o Telegram degli amici
  • Screenshot dei messaggi più sgrammaticati
  • Foto di celebrità o personaggi iconici
  • Foto di gatti
  • Foto di gatti arrabbiati
  • Foto di gatti arrabbiati satanici

4. Condivisione

Una volta salvato il calendario su CodePen:

  • Clicca in alto a destra per cambiare la “vista” e seleziona “Full Page View”.
  • Condividi l’URL della pagina con chi vuoi via chat, social o email.

Se hai competenze di web development, puoi spingerti oltre e modificare anche il resto codice, non essere timido!

6. Conclusione

Creare un calendario dell’avvento digitale è divertente e alla portata di tutti.
In poco tempo puoi realizzare una piccola sorpresa quotidiana per amici e parenti, senza limitarti ai cioccolatini (che fameee 😭).
Basta trovare 24 immagini e qualche minuto di tempo.

Se decidi di creare il tuo calendario, condividilo anche qua sotto: voglio vedere le vostre creazioni, in particolare quelle con Jessica Alba (ma non era mica Jessica Nigri prima? 🤔).

Sei arrivato fin qui e non hai capito nulla?

medium.titulo: Using Customer Feedback to Prioritize Design System Improvements
medium.resumo: Build a design system roadmap from customer needs, support evidence, accessibility findings, and adoption friction with clear priorities…
medium.conteudo_html:
Build a design system roadmap from customer needs, support evidence, accessibility findings, and adoption friction with clear priorities and measurable outcomes.

Customer feedback helps a design system team discover where shared components and patterns are failing in real products. A request for another table option may reveal a difficult reporting task. Repeated questions about a form component may point to missing guidance, an unsuitable API, or an accessibility barrier. The first step is to understand the problem behind the requested change.

Effective design system prioritization connects that problem to evidence, affected users, implementation cost, and an observable outcome. A clear process lets teams decide which improvements belong in the shared system, which need product-specific work, and which require more research before engineering begins.

Collect feedback from customers and consuming teams

A design system has at least two important audiences: the designers and engineers who build with it, and the people who use the resulting products. Developer feedback explains integration friction; customer research explains whether the completed experience works. Review both before concluding that a component request represents a broader need.

  • Support reports: identify blocked tasks, confusing messages, recurring workarounds, and recovery failures.
  • Usability research: observe how people understand and operate patterns in a complete journey.
  • Accessibility evaluations: identify keyboard, focus, naming, contrast, and assistive technology barriers.
  • Integration issues: collect component versions, framework details, reproducible examples, and unexpected API behavior.
  • Adoption reviews: investigate local forks, duplicate components, abandoned migrations, and missing documentation.

Give these channels one shared tracking process without requiring everyone to use the same reporting tool. A support team can submit a structured summary on behalf of a customer. Keep sensitive account details and research recordings in access-controlled systems, and use sanitized descriptions in broadly visible planning records.

Use a feedback intake template that captures the problem

Ask for enough detail to investigate, while keeping the reporting effort manageable. Reproduction steps are especially useful for defects; proposed enhancements need the task, current limitation, and evidence of repeated need. Do not make a fully developed solution a prerequisite for reporting a barrier.

Component or pattern: Data table
Installed version: Record the affected release
Affected task: Review selected invoices across multiple pages
Observed problem: Selection state is unclear after pagination
Expected outcome: Users can identify and review selected invoices
Evidence:
- Minimal reproduction or sanitized recording
- Browser, input method, and relevant environment
- Independent teams or products reporting the same behavior
- Research observations, where available
Current workaround: Separate application-level selection summary
Impact: Additional implementation work and user confusion
Owner: Design system triage team
Next action: Reproduce and classify the underlying issue

Separate observed facts from interpretations. “Three teams implemented separate selection summaries” is evidence. “Every customer needs a new table component” is a conclusion that still needs validation. Record uncertainty explicitly so the roadmap does not turn an early assumption into an engineering commitment.

Group related reports without losing important context

Create a problem record for a repeated theme and associate individual reports with it. Preserve differences in component version, device, task, and integration. Similar symptoms can have different causes: one focus failure may originate in a shared dialog, while another comes from how an application opens it.

Count independent affected teams and known usage contexts rather than raw message volume. Ten follow-up comments on one ticket are not ten separate customers. At the same time, low reporting volume does not establish low impact. A barrier that prevents a smaller group from completing a critical task can deserve immediate action.

Review the problem record with product teams before choosing a shared solution. The best intervention might be a documentation example, an integration fix, a component patch, a new pattern, or a product-specific change. Expanding a public API should follow a demonstrated need and a maintenance plan.

Build a design system prioritization rubric

Begin with severity triage. Critical task blockers and serious regressions need an explicit response path rather than waiting for a weighted backlog score. Then compare planned improvements using a consistent rubric. The following dimensions are a practical starting point that a team can adapt to its own product portfolio.

  • User impact: whether the issue blocks completion, creates errors, slows a task, or causes minor friction.
  • Reach: independently affected products, teams, and usage contexts, with unknown reach clearly marked.
  • Evidence confidence: reproducible defects and observed research findings versus an untested request.
  • Workaround cost: repeated application code, support burden, maintenance, and the quality of available alternatives.
  • Strategic fit: connection to agreed product goals, supported patterns, and current platform commitments.
  • Total effort: research, implementation, testing, documentation, migration, and ongoing support.

If the team uses scores, publish definitions for each level and keep the rationale beside the result. Avoid presenting a rough estimate as a precise prediction. Two similarly ranked items may need a small discovery task to reduce uncertainty before either enters delivery. Review dependencies and available capacity alongside the score.

Shared value also matters when deciding whether to add a component. The GOV.UK Design System contribution criteria ask for evidence of usefulness across teams and consider whether a proposal duplicates existing patterns. These are useful questions for evaluating whether a customer request belongs in a reusable system.

Example: prioritize a table improvement over a cosmetic variant

Consider two hypothetical requests. One asks for an additional decorative badge style used by a single product. The other reports that users cannot reliably understand which invoices remain selected when changing table pages. Several consuming teams have implemented their own selection summaries.

Investigate the table behavior first if evidence confirms that it disrupts an important task. Reproduce it in the shared component and in an application to establish ownership. Determine whether the missing behavior belongs to the table primitive or to a higher-level selection pattern. This avoids adding unrelated responsibilities to the core API.

Define acceptance criteria before implementation

  • Selection persistence follows an explicit rule across pagination and filtering.
  • Users can identify selected items and review or clear them using supported input methods.
  • Bulk actions explain which items they affect and provide appropriate recovery or confirmation.
  • Loading, empty, partial-selection, and error states have documented behavior.
  • Consuming teams can adopt the change with clear compatibility and migration guidance.

The badge request can still receive a useful response. An existing token or composition pattern might satisfy it, or the request may remain under consideration until broader need appears. Explain that decision and what new evidence would change it.

Publish a roadmap with decisions and next steps

Give each feedback item a meaningful status such as received, investigating, planned, in progress, released, or declined. Distinguish “needs evidence” from “will not pursue” so reporters understand whether they can help move the discussion forward. Assign an owner and a next review point for active investigations.

A Now, Next, and Later roadmap can communicate direction without implying a delivery date for every idea. Include the problem being addressed, intended outcome, dependencies, and reason for priority. Keep confidential customer evidence separate from the explanation shared with the wider community.

Set an acknowledgement target the team can maintain and explain how urgent barriers should be raised. Acknowledgement confirms that a report is being reviewed; it should not be confused with a promise to deliver a fix within the same period.

Include component quality and migration in the delivery plan

Validate proposed behavior with consuming teams before finalizing the API. Create examples for the states reported in feedback, then review keyboard operation, accessible names, responsive content, and integration boundaries. Add automated regression checks where they can verify the behavior, together with manual assessment for qualities they cannot prove.

Account for design assets, documentation, release notes, and consumer upgrades as part of the work. A breaking change needs explicit migration instructions and a realistic transition plan. If the system supports several framework packages, track parity and compatibility rather than assuming a fix in one implementation reaches all consumers.

Close the feedback loop after release

Tell reporters which release contains the improvement, what changed, and what they need to do to adopt it. Ask affected teams to verify the result in their real workflow. Mark the implementation as released while tracking adoption separately; a merged pull request does not establish that the customer’s barrier has been removed.

Feedback becomes valuable when a reported problem leads to an explainable decision and a verified outcome.

For declined or deferred items, provide the reasoning and a supported alternative where one exists. Review unresolved themes periodically because new adoption evidence or product changes can alter the decision. Keep the history available so new team members do not have to reconstruct the same discussion.

Measure whether design system improvements reach users

Combine process measures with outcome measures. Fast acknowledgement is useful, but it cannot show whether the system became easier to use. Establish a baseline for each major improvement and identify when the team will review the result.

  • Triage health: time to acknowledgement, time to a decision, and age of unresolved high-impact reports.
  • Adoption: affected applications using the corrected component or recommended pattern.
  • Repeated work: reduction in local workarounds and duplicated implementation effort.
  • Quality: recurrence of the original defect, new regressions, and verified accessibility barriers.
  • User outcomes: observed task completion, recovery difficulties, and support contacts related to the reported problem.

Interpret trends within their context. Fewer reports might mean improvement, lower usage, or difficulty finding the reporting channel. Compare equivalent periods and review qualitative evidence alongside counts. Avoid ranking individual teams by ticket volume, since active reporting can indicate healthy participation.

Start with a small, repeatable feedback review

Choose one recurring component problem, gather its independent reports, and confirm the underlying need. Apply the rubric, publish the decision, and define the smallest useful improvement. Reserve capacity for validation and consumer adoption as well as implementation.

After release, review the evidence with reporters and update the backlog accordingly. Repeating this cycle gives the roadmap a clear connection to customer needs while keeping the design system coherent, maintainable, and useful across products.

corrida_no_ar.titulo: MARATONA DO RIO entra no TOP 10 mundial pela segunda vez
corrida_no_ar.resumo: Maratona do Rio é novamente Top 10 mundial, esclarecemos as regras sobre o número de peito, nova collab Olympikus e Guaraná, e o temporal em Maringá que adiou a etapa do Circuito Sesc. Aproveite os cupons de desconto para a Uphill Corcovado e o Mountain Do.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quinta-feira | 5 de novembro de 2026

A Maratona do Rio foi considerada, pela segunda vez, a 10ª prova de 42 km com a marca mais forte do mundo. O ranking foi divulgado pela consultoria britânica Brand Finance, que avaliou o impacto econômico e a força das marcas das 50 principais maratonas globais. No total, essas corridas geram cerca de US$ 6 bilhões para as cidades-sede. A Maratona de Londres lidera como a marca mais forte, seguida por Nova York, Boston, Berlin e Paris. O Top 10 ainda conta com Tóquio, Sydney, Chicago, Amsterdam e, fechando a lista, a Maratona do Rio de Janeiro.

Apesar da força da marca, no quesito impacto econômico, a prova carioca ficou na 29ª posição, gerando US$ 44 milhões. Em comparação, a Maratona de Londres, que lidera também neste ranking, movimenta US$ 857 milhões.

Para quem valem as regras de competição?

Muitas pessoas questionam a aplicação das regras de competição, como a que define o uso do número de peito. É importante esclarecer que a corrida de rua faz parte do atletismo, um esporte com regras técnicas e de competição bem definidas. Em provas com participação em massa, como as corridas de rua, essas regras devem ser aplicadas integralmente aos atletas que estão competindo pela elite ou por prêmios em suas categorias de faixa etária. O prêmio pode ser em dinheiro, troféu ou qualquer outra forma de reconhecimento.

A regra sobre o número de peito é clara: durante a competição, ele deve ser usado visivelmente na “frente do tronco”. Colocá-lo no shorts, na virilha ou nas costas é uma infração que pode levar à desclassificação. Para corredores que não estão competindo por pódio e correm de forma participativa, a fiscalização costuma ser mais branda, mas a regra existe e se aplica a quem está na disputa.

Inscrições abertas para a Uphill Corcovado

Estão abertas as inscrições para a Uphill Corcovado, que acontece no dia 21 de novembro no Rio de Janeiro. A prova é uma oportunidade única de ver a cidade iluminada do alto, correndo à noite. Com percursos de 5K, 10K e 21K, o evento promete uma experiência incrível. Para quem quiser participar, o Corrida no Ar oferece um cupom de 30% de desconto: use “CORRIDANOAR30” no momento da inscrição.

Olympikus e Guaraná Antarctica lançam collab

A Olympikus anunciou uma parceria inédita com o Guaraná Antarctica, resultando em uma edição especial do tênis Corre 5. A colaboração celebra duas marcas brasileiras, com o design do calçado inspirado no fruto do guaraná, originário de Maués, no Amazonas. O tênis apresenta tons de verde e vermelho, característicos da fruta. O lançamento é uma edição limitada e já está disponível para venda.

Chuvas em Maringá adiam prova do Sesc

As fortes chuvas e ventos que atingiram Maringá, no Paraná, forçaram o adiamento da etapa do Circuito Sesc de Corridas, que estava prevista para o próximo domingo, 8 de novembro. A organização ainda divulgará uma nova data para o evento. Em relação à Maratona de Maringá, marcada para o dia 21 de novembro, os organizadores informaram que a prova está mantida. Eles garantem que, apesar da destruição causada pelo temporal na cidade, haverá tempo suficiente para reparar os danos e, se necessário, fazer pequenas alterações nos percursos de 5K e 10K para garantir a segurança de todos.

Uma experiência única no Mountain Do

A etapa da Chapada dos Veadeiros do circuito Mountain Do, que aconteceu recentemente, foi um sucesso, proporcionando aos corredores uma experiência incrível com visuais deslumbrantes. O evento é conhecido pela organização cuidadosa, segurança e percursos desafiadores. Se você quer viver uma aventura como essa, aproveite o cupom “CORRIDANOAR” para ter 10% de desconto na sua inscrição em qualquer etapa do circuito.
